title: Allegorical Reading
lead: Allegory reads a text as saying one thing and meaning another. Jews and Christians used it to read the Song of Songs as the love of God for Israel, or of Christ for the Church or the soul. The Church of the Fathers held that Scripture has a literal sense and spiritual senses, the allegorical, moral and anagogical, all resting on the literal. Antiochene writers such as Theodore of Mopsuestia stressed the plain sense; the Reformers returned to it, and modern scholars mostly read the Song as love poetry.

sections.h: Allegory in the Bible and the early church
sections.b: Paul himself speaks of Sarah and Hagar as an allegory (Galatians 4:21–31) and reads the story of the exodus as an example for the church (1 Corinthians 10:1–11). Origen of Alexandria (about AD 185–253), in a commentary and two homilies on the Song, used the Song to show how the soul's love for the Word grows through stages. His method shaped Latin and Greek exegesis for a thousand years, and Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) preached eighty-six sermons on the Song that reach only 3:1.
sections.refs: Galatians 4:21–31; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Hebrews 8:5; Song of Songs 1:2

sections.h: The plain sense and the return to it
sections.b: Theodore of Mopsuestia (about AD 350–428) is reported to have rejected the allegory and read the Song as Solomon's love poem for Pharaoh's daughter; later writers use this report to say he was condemned for it, a claim that depends on the sources. Sebastian Castellio is said to have called the Song a lascivious poem in Geneva in 1544. Luther read it as Solomon's praise of good government, and the Puritans read it as the love of Christ for the believer. Modern scholars read it first as poetry about human love, and many Jewish and Catholic teachers still allow the allegorical reading real weight.
